title: First In, First Out? Birth Order and Next-Generation Engagement in Family Firms
authors: Mohamed Genedy; Lucia Naldi; Karin Hellerstedt
affiliations: House of Innovation (HOI), Stockholm School of Economics, Sweden; Jönköping International Business School, Centre for Family Entrepreneurship and Ownership (CeFEO), Jönköping University, Sweden; IE University, Spain
abstract: Research shows that next-generation engagement in the family business is important for the business’s long-term survival. However, the literature has neglected how differences among children could explain their career choices in the family business. We address this gap by drawing on birth order theory to examine differences in three career choices of the next-generation: joining the family business, holding a managerial position, and leaving the family business. Using a sample from Sweden, we employ family-stratified hazard models and show that later-borns are more likely to join the family business as their initial career choice compared to earlier-born siblings. However, when the next-generation joins the family business, later-borns are less likely to hold managerial positions in the family business and more likely to leave the family business. We conduct several mechanism tests explaining our hypotheses and run additional robustness tests to support our results. This study advances the research on next-generation engagement in family firms.

title: Platform development in incumbent firms: The interplay of data and actor interests in adding platforms to existing businesses
authors: Jack Fraser; Elizabeth J. Altman; Pinar Ozcan
affiliations: Imperial Business School Imperial College London London UK; Manning School of Business University of Massachusetts Lowell Lowell Massachusetts USA; Saïd Business School University of Oxford Oxford UK
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Despite growing interest in platform transitions, limited research examines how firms navigate challenges of building platform businesses alongside existing products. Through a longitudinal case study of a financial services firm launching a platform, we develop a process model revealing how data bottlenecks shape platform development. These bottlenecks arise from the interplay of technological limitations and control tensions over data aggregation, sharing, and usage. We identify five sequential bottlenecks, where resolving one reconfigures constraints, giving rise to the next. We theorize how data heterogeneity, variation in strategic sensitivity, and actors' absorptive capacity create opportunities for platform sponsors to capture value without competing with complementors. We extend resource dependency theory by showing how peripheral units overcome power imbalances by demonstrating value creation potential with limited data. Managerial Summary When established firms launch platforms alongside existing product businesses, they face significant data‐related obstacles. Drawing on a four‐year study of a financial services firm building a platform connecting SMEs with lenders, we show how firms must navigate challenges in collecting data from internal units and customers, making incompatible data sources work together, and persuading partners to share and use data in new ways. We find that these obstacles emerge in sequence, where resolving one creates the conditions for the next. We also find that not all data is equally useful to all partners, and that these differences can open market segments the platform sponsor can serve without competing with its own partners. Managers can maintain momentum by combining short‐term data workarounds with longer‐term structural solutions.

title: Connective Resource Mobilization: A Relational Approach to Movement Continuity in Transnational Activism
authors: Pamela P. Tsui
affiliations: University of Toronto
abstract: Social movement studies have long centered social movement organizations (SMOs) as the primary vehicles of mobilization. Yet contemporary movements are increasingly decentralized and digitally mediated, challenging SMO-centric frameworks such as resource mobilization theory (RMT). As contention becomes more individualized and non-conventional, organization- and event-centered approaches struggle to explain how movements persist, evolve, or dissolve under shifting conditions. Drawing on RMT and economic sociology, this article advances a relational resource mobilization framework through four propositions: resource mobilization (1) is historically contingent; (2) translates into tactics differently across organizational configurations; (3) is relational; and (4) provides an analytic for examining movement continuity across time and space. Within this framework, I introduce the model of connective resource mobilization to theorize how digitally mediated movements generate strategic capacity through personalized earmarking practices across borders and phases of contention. Based on 179 interviews and observation at 187 events in Hong Kong and Canada, I trace how the Hong Kong Pro-Democracy Movement evolved from its 2019 protest peak through its subsequent downturn across domestic and diasporic contexts. The analysis demonstrates how a relational approach to resource mobilization can illuminate divergent trajectories of movement continuity across historical, geographic, political, and socio-technological contexts.

title: Small Polity, Hybrid Administration, International Research: Public Administration in Switzerland
authors: Fritz Sager; Adrian Ritz; Johanna Hornung
affiliations: University of Bern Bern Switzerland; University of Lausanne Lausanne Switzerland
abstract: ABSTRACT Switzerland presents a most peculiar political system whose institutional idiosyncrasies shape not only the practice of public administration but also the scientific study thereof. This country study presents the development and state of both public administration as practice and Public Administration as a scholarly discipline. It argues that both are largely determined by three properties of Switzerland as a political context and field of study: Semi‐direct democracy turns the administration into an important political actor. The “Milizsystem” (Switzerland's tradition of non‐professionalized, part‐time public engagement) enables hybrid careers between the public and private sectors and produces a structurally weaker political class that the professional administration regularly outmaneuvers. And the small size of the country has pushed the discipline toward international orientation while simultaneously entangling researchers with their object of study. Taken together, the Swiss case illustrates how political institutions do not merely constrain public administration but fundamentally constitute it.

title:
The
                    <scp>DOGE</scp>
                    Experiment: Algorithmic Governance, Operational Capture, and the Case for Hybrid Intelligence
authors: Haris Alibašić
affiliations: Department of Business Administration Lewis Bear Jr. College of Business, University of West Florida Pensacola Florida USA
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) as a case of algorithmic governance whose stated purpose, improving federal efficiency, diverged systematically from its operational effect: enabling unprecedented private‐sector access to federal data systems while dismantling the oversight and civil‐service infrastructure that constrains such access. Drawing on state capacity, bounded rationality, organizational learning, and public value theory, the analysis demonstrates that the conventional efficiency‐failure reading, though correct on its own terms, obscures what made DOGE structurally distinct from the Grace Commission, the National Performance Review, the President's Management Agenda, and Program Assessment Rating Tool, and the Government Performance and Results Modernization Act. The article advances hybrid intelligence, structured human‐AI collaboration with protected institutional capacity, as a paradigm resisting both reform failure and algorithmic capture. International implementations operationalize it. The analysis contributes a stated‐versus‐operational‐goal analytic to the AI governance literature and identifies legislative grounding as a precondition for durable reform.

title: What Does Representation Represent? Disaggregating Demographic and Behavioral Components
authors: Rachel (Soyeon) Cho
affiliations: School of Public Affairs American University Washington District of Columbia USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Representative bureaucracy research has often linked demographic representation directly to favorable outcomes, inferring active representation post hoc while rarely separating the behavioral component presumed to accompany such associations from the representation variable itself. This study addresses such gap by drawing on gender differences in leadership literature to operationalize supportive leadership as one behavioral component associated with female supervisory representation and examine the constituent elements of what has been interpreted as a representation effect. Using gender pay inequality across US federal agencies as the empirical context, the findings show that while both female supervisory representation and supportive leadership are each positively associated with nonsupervisory salaries when examined separately, the association attributed to representation loses significance once both are modeled together. These findings do not suggest that representation is unimportant; rather, they indicate that prior representation effects may partially reflect a behavioral component that has not been separately identified.

title: Correction to “Celebrating 86 Years”
Skills, Not Just Will: Experimental Evidence From Uganda on Transparency in Public Procurement
authors: Mark T. Buntaine; Alex Bagabo; Paul Bukuluki; Brigham Daniels; Gerald Padde Auku
affiliations: Bren School of Environmental Science & Management University of California Santa Barbara California USA; Department of Social Work and Social Administration, School of Social Sciences Makerere University Kampala Uganda; S.J. Quinney College of Law University of Utah Salt Lake City Utah USA; Transparency International Uganda Kampala Uganda
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments are usually the largest purchasers of goods and services, creating significant opportunities for corruption. We study whether offering training and technical assistance to procurement officials in 50 Ugandan districts prompted them to publish procurement actions on an online public portal, as legally required. Among districts that received the training and technical assistance program, we randomized whether procurement officials received information in advance about their eligibility to earn a public award for adherence to these transparency standards. We use national administrative data across multiple financial years and 134 district governments to evaluate impacts. The training and technical assistance program increased the number and value of procurement actions uploaded several‐fold, while award eligibility did not have similarly large effects. These results suggest that motivation problems may be overemphasized in the fight against corruption. Building capacity in accounting and transparency could provide effective guardrails against corruption.

title: Two-Sided Pricing and Learning with Buyer Choice: A Generalized SGD Method
authors: Meichun Lin; Woonghee Tim Huh
affiliations: Lee Kong Chian School of Business, Singapore Management University, Singapore 178899; Sauder School of Business, The University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia V6T 1Z4, Canada
abstract: Learning to Price in Two-Sided Markets Many two-sided platforms set purchase prices for sellers and selling prices for buyers. In “Two-Sided Pricing and Learning with Buyer Choice: A Generalized SGD Method,” Lin and Huh study how platforms can make these decisions when responses on both sides are uncertain and must be learned from limited data. They first show that, when supply and demand models are known, simple fixed-price policies that match expected supply and demand can be asymptotically optimal. Building on this insight, the authors develop a novel generalization of classical stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for learning a fixed-price policy. Unlike standard SGD, their method does not require the construction of a strongly convex objective function. This flexibility allows it to accommodate demand interactions arising from buyer choice. The resulting learning algorithm is near-optimal when the planning horizon is large.

title: Generative Search: Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
authors: Shuang Zheng; Yuting Zhu; Xin Ye; Liang Shen
affiliations: School of Business, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100086, China; and DUT School of Economics and Management, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian City 116024, China; and Meituan, Beijing 100102, China; NUS Business School, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119245; DUT School of Economics and Management, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian City 116024, China; Meituan, Beijing 100102, China
abstract: Generative search is an emerging search paradigm that integrates Generative AI (GenAI) into traditional search engines by presenting users with AI-generated responses before conventional search results. Whereas keyword-based search requires consumers to translate their underlying needs into effective keyword queries, generative search lets users express those intentions directly in natural language, a shift made possible by GenAI’s new mode of information presentation. This shift moves the consumer-search engine interaction upstream to the stage of problem formulation, rendering empirically observable a previously hidden phase of search behavior: the mapping from problem formulation to keyword articulation. Yet, it remains empirically unknown whether generative search increases consumer purchases and how search behavior changes when it can begin from expressed intent rather than keywords. Using a large-scale field experiment conducted on Meituan, a leading Chinese technology platform, this paper provides empirical evidence on the effectiveness of generative search. We find that generative search significantly increases consumer purchases. Further analysis reveals that generative search facilitates more effective and diverse keyword queries and reduces exploratory browsing and clicking, while concentrating evaluation within relevant categories and merchants. The empirical evidence is most consistent with a mechanism in which AI-generated answers provide information about consumers’ underlying needs, while also expanding awareness of relevant attributes and shifting attention toward more relevant categories. These findings provide empirical insights for future consumer search models that allow search to originate at the intention-expressing stage. This paper was accepted by Raphael Thomadsen, marketing. Funding: Financial support from the Ministry of Education – Singapore [Grant A-8001730-00-00] is gratefully acknowledged. title: Remedial Labour and the materialities of housing precarity: Homemaking in informal subdivided units
authors: Ruby YS Lai
affiliations: Lingnan University, Hong Kong S.A.R
abstract: The global housing crisis has rendered housing insecure and inadequate in sustaining family life and dignified living. Housing precarity is not merely a situation to live in but also to live with , requiring constant negotiation with housing difficulties across spatial, temporal and relational dimensions. Building on years of ethnographic fieldwork, I utilise the literature of materiality to uncover the invisible labour of tenants living in subdivided units in Hong Kong, that is, tiny informal compartments constructed through unauthorised apartment subdivision. I conceptualise this domestic work as remedial labour – the everyday necessary remedy to defective dwellings – in which tenants transform their inadequate space into a habitable home. This exploration illuminates how the state governmentality and housing regime have jointly destabilised individuals’ home experiences and exemplifies the way in which tenants’ everyday labour buffers the societal consequences of the housing crisis and infrastructural failures resulting from market-oriented urban and housing governance.

title: A Replication of “It is Not Merely About the Content: How Rules Are Communicated Matters to Administrative Burden”
authors: Qi Bian; Luning Xin; Ben Ma
affiliations: School of Political Science and Public Administration Shandong University Qingdao Shandong China; Smart State Governance Lab Shandong University Qingdao Shandong China
abstract: ABSTRACT This study replicates prior research to examine how rule communication forms shape administrative burden, while also extending their research by investigating how artificial intelligence (AI) services moderate this relationship. AI services are understood to perform two distinct functions: the labeling function, where chatbots output policy rules directly from databases in response to user queries without further processing, and the optimization function, where chatbots collect, analyze, and distill rule information to present users with simplified, prioritized key points. In Study 1, the original research is replicated in the context of natural disaster relief applications in China. The findings demonstrate that bureaucratic language raises learning and compliance costs, stress, and autonomy loss, while complex information structures also increase learning costs, compliance costs, and autonomy loss. These results confirm that rule communication shapes administrative burden across policies, countries, and languages. However, differences emerge compared to the original study, in which bureaucratic language induced stigma and information complexity had no effect on compliance or autonomy loss, potentially due to contextual factors such as the complexity of Chinese logographic writing. Building on this, the extension experiment in Study 2 demonstrates that AI services reduce administrative burden. Notably, and contrary to expectations, the labeling function reduces learning, compliance, and psychological costs, while the optimization function achieves even greater reductions across all dimensions. Collectively, these findings provide empirical evidence supporting the use of AI to improve rule communication and ease administrative burden.

title: EXPRESS: Pay Transparency and Inequality Concerns: Productivity and Job Satisfaction
authors: Lin Chen; Antoine Désir; Guillaume Roels
abstract: Although pay transparency is generally effective at reducing the gender gap, it is not without downsides, sometimes leading to reduced productivity and lower job satisfaction due to inequality concerns. Yet, workers could have different objects of comparison: income, utility, or rewards. Across these different types of inequality concerns, when does pay transparency result in both higher output and fair outcomes? We consider a model of moral hazard involving a principal and two agents of heterogeneous abilities who are averse to inequalities between each other. We study three bases of comparison: income, utility, and reward. Anticipating the agents’ change in behavior as a result of pay transparency, the principal adjusts the terms of their output-sharing contract with them. We find that pay transparency under income comparison never benefits the principal and might give rise to feelings of guilt and envy—thus reducing agents’ utility. In contrast, under reward comparison, it is always beneficial to the principal and results in fair outcomes. Under utility comparison, it lies somewhere in between, offering a higher payoff and fair outcomes when agents are not so heterogeneous, but hurting them without changing the principal’s payoff otherwise. In sum, we find that pay transparency has the potential for increasing productivity without negative feelings of fairness. However, the object of comparison matters. Therefore, it is paramount for organizations to contextualize income information to shift employees' concerns away from income to either utility or reward considerations by adopting process transparency in addition to outcome transparency.

title: EXPRESS: Gain by Letting Go: Environmental Investments and Profitability of Benefit Corporations
authors: Baozhuang Niu; Yiyuan Ruan; Luyi Gui; Nan Zhang
abstract: Benefit corporation is a new legal status of for-profit companies, which requires statutory commitment to public benefit purposes. The adoption of benefit corporation rather than a traditional C corporation is generally regarded as a tradeoff: a benefit corporation is believed to invest more in responsible business practices at the expense of profit compared to a profit-maximizing C corporation counterpart. In this paper, we examine the validity of this perspective from a supply chain perspective, focusing on a consumer goods brand that pledges to reduce total emissions as its public benefit purpose. We develop parsimonious models of the brand's emission reduction investment and product distribution decisions when it sells to consumers directly, indirectly via a retailer, or both. Through a comparison of the optimal decisions when the brand is incorporated as a benefit corporation versus a profit-maximizing C corporation, we show that converting to a benefit corporation intensifies the rebound effect associated with carbon footprint reduction, and thereby may reduce the brand's investment in such reductions when it strongly emphasizes total emission abatement in its objective. A moderate focus on profit can mitigate this problem and enhance a benefit corporation's investment in carbon footprint reduction especially under dual distribution channels. Furthermore, the brand can be more profitable as a benefit corporation than as a profit-maximizing C corporation under dual distribution channels, as the benefit corporation status increases channel differentiation and softens competition. Our study indicates that profit and public benefit objectives may reinforce each other. A well-balanced corporate goal can lay plausible grounds for mitigating profit concerns and shareholder pushback to the benefit corporation status, as well as for increasing environmental investment incentives derived from that status. In addition, policies that help benefit corporations access market through differentiated dual channels can be pathways to improve their financial viability and public benefit impacts.

title: EXPRESS: Single vs. Variable Pricing under Uncertainty with Limited Capacity
authors: Chunlin Wang; Huaqing (Mike) Wang; Haresh Gurnani; Saibal Ray
abstract: This paper studies a firm's pricing strategies under joint uncertainty in costs and demand (market size), with potential capacity constraints. We organize four pricing strategies along a single dimension: the amount and type of realized information a firm commits its pricing rule to use, ranging from none, under single pricing , to both cost and demand , under the most flexible strategy; between these extremes, demand-based pricing conditions price on realized demand alone, and cost-based pricing conditions price on realized cost alone. We examine the implications of this informational flexibility for three stakeholders: the firm, consumers, and society. We note that, across all capacity levels, the firm’s profit is maximized by the most flexible pricing strategy, namely, pricing based on both cost and demand realizations. In contrast, the pricing strategy that maximizes consumer surplus and social welfare depends on the severity of the capacity constraint. Under tight capacity, demand-based pricing and pricing based on both cost and demand realizations dominate. However, when capacity is sufficiently large (i.e., an uncapacitated setting), cost-based pricing maximizes consumer surplus and social welfare. Interestingly, for intermediate capacity levels, single pricing might be the best option for both consumers and society, even though it commits the firm to using the least information. The above results are robust to both discrete and continuous demand distributions. We further show that when costs and demand are positively correlated, single pricing still might be socially optimal. Overall, the paper shows how the information a pricing rule commits to use interacts with capacity constraints to shape the profit and welfare effects of pricing flexibility, offering guidance on when each strategy is likely to be favorable for the stakeholders.

title: Modern Slavery in Supply Chains: A Framing Perspective on Managerial Responses to Transparency Legislation
authors: Bruce Pinnington; Alexandra Williams‐Woods
affiliations: Management School University of Liverpool Liverpool UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Innovative legislation aspires for an extra‐jurisdictional effect on modern slavery in supply chains through increased transparency. Evidence to date suggests that firms are not rising to this challenge, and, if anything, mandatory reporting practices are coalescing around superficial reports decoupled from policy objectives. To decide how the regulatory regime should best be adapted, it is important to understand not just the organizational‐level response but also the underlying managerial attitudes and behavior on which substantive practical action depends. The study utilized a photo elicitation method with 47 managers drawn from eight large UK construction firms. Framing theory was utilized to reveal four distinct managerial mindsets, each with different implications for policy and practice. These variants suggest that a one‐size‐fits‐all policy approach is suboptimal. Policy combining rewards and penalties, tailored to each framing group, is likely to be the most expedient in quickly improving managerial behavior. The existence of inconsistent framing within firms suggests that strategic policies are not being effectively embedded in managerial practice. In turn, this limits the impact that focal firms have in improving labor practices across multiple tiers of their supply chains. Reporting entities should not be treated as cohesive, unitary entities by stakeholders.

title: Adaptive management control systems in operations: the reconfiguration of control mechanisms on the shop floor
authors: Allan Hansen; Michael Güldenpfennig; Kim Sundtoft Hald
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School Department of Operations Management, , ,
abstract: Purpose This paper investigates the complexity and dynamics of assembly line managers' management control systems. It examines which mechanisms comprise these systems and how their relevance and configuration change as managers tackle different productivity-related control problems on the shop floor. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts an abductive single case study approach, drawing on interview, observational and archival data from a global automotive supplier. Building on complexity theory and management control research, it analyses line managers' control problems on a U-shaped assembly line. Findings The study identifies three recurrent workforce-related control problems (workforce assignment, managing process interruptions and motivating the team) and shows how five types of management control mechanisms (administrative, cultural, cybernetic, planning and reward) combine into distinct configurations around each control problem. These configurations shift as managers' attention moves between control problems, representing dynamics that can be interpreted through the lens of a complex adaptive system. Practical implications By demonstrating how line managers combine and reconfigure control mechanisms across recurring control problems, this study offers actionable insights for line manager training and for senior managers seeking to support shop floor productivity. Originality/value This study interprets management control systems in operations as complex adaptive systems and introduces the notion of control problem dynamics, showing how shop floor productivity management emerges through the co-evolution of control mechanisms and the control problems they address.

title: Trade Exposure and the Decline in Collective Bargaining: Evidence From Germany
authors: Daniel Baumgarten; Sybille Lehwald
affiliations: Paderborn University, CESifo and RWI Paderborn Germany; Federal Chancellery Berlin Germany
abstract: ABSTRACT We analyze how rising trade exposure from China and Eastern Europe affected collective bargaining coverage in German plants from 1996 to 2008. Using cross‐industry variation in trade exposure and instrumenting with trade flows from other high‐income countries, we find that higher import exposure increased the likelihood that plants exited industry‐wide bargaining agreements, while export exposure had no average effect. Overall, rising trade exposure explains about 13% of the decline in industry‐wide bargaining coverage. The import effect is stronger for small and medium‐sized plants, while export opportunities help stabilize participation among large plants and those with works councils.

title: Propagation of Immigration Shocks through Firm-to-Firm Trade Networks,
authors: Yusuf Emre Akgündüz; Abdurrahman B Aydemir; Seyit Mümin Cilasun; Murat Güray Kirdar
affiliations: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey , Istanbul ,; Sabanci University, Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences , Istanbul ,; TED University , Ankara ,; Koç University, College of Administrative Sciences and Economics , Istanbul ,
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the extent to which an immigration shock to a region propagates through supply chains. Using the unexpected arrival of Syrian refugees, who are densely concentrated in border regions of Turkey, we estimate how firms across the country are affected in terms of sales, employment, and wages. We also examine the impact of the shock on interprovincial trade, focusing on trade volume and network formation. The results reveal positive spillover effects of immigration for firms with pre-existing links to Syrian refugee-hosting regions through upstream and downstream supply chain connections. Furthermore, we find evidence that the shock expands inter-provincial trade and contributes to the formation of new firm-to-firm linkages between provinces. Finally, we show that traditional spatial approaches that compare regions with differing migration rates may conflate cross-province propagation with the direct effect of migrants; in our setting, this conflation overstates direct effects on sales and employment at both the firm and regional levels of aggregation and masks a negative direct wage effect at the firm level.

title: Gustav Schmoller and the German Historical School: Revisiting the Intellectual Roots of Business History at Harvard
authors: Matthias Störring
affiliations: Global Ethic Institute at the University of Tübingen
abstract: Abstract This article traces the intellectual lineage between the German Historical School of Political Economy—particularly the work of Gustav Schmoller—and the formation of business history at Harvard Business School. It reconstructs a connection that remains insufficiently recognized in accounts of the discipline’s origins, situating its emergence within a broader transatlantic exchange of ideas and academic practices around the turn of the twentieth century. The article shows how Schmoller’s approach to political economy informed early business education at Harvard through key intermediaries such as William J. Ashley and Edwin F. Gay, and how these influences were subsequently embraced and advanced within the Harvard milieu. Focusing on the divergent yet complementary contributions of N. S. B. Gras and Arthur H. Cole, it highlights Harvard’s role as an intellectual incubator rather than a point of origin. In doing so, the article recovers a genealogy of business history and considers its implications for the field’s self-understanding.

title: Libraries, research and development funding, and economic prosperity: data for the holistic university
authors: R. Eugene Turner; Suzanne L. Marchand
abstract: Abstract Macro indicators of Research and Development (R&D) such as numbers of journal publications and citation rates, patents, impact factors, and R&D expenditures have become proxies for economic competitiveness. But quantifying relationships between macro-indicators and budgets supporting these indirect metrics of R&D are sparse, and some factors critical to the holistic university, such as expenditures on libraries, have been missed. We quantified post-1945 relationships between federal research and development (R&D) funding to large universities and individual university rankings and regional economic prosperity in the United States. Empirical data, substantiated by a principal component analysis of multiple additional university-specific factors, reveals that there are $21.34 of R&D expenditures for each $1 of library expenditures at 71 public universities; arts and humanities programs are a positive influence for acquiring R&D funds. University rankings for > 90 universities are also positively correlated to R&D expenditures. There is a $1:$264 ratio of state-wide R&D expenditures to state’s gross economic production ( R 2 = 0.86), and a $1:$59 ratio for a state’s per capita R&D expenditure vs. per capita income ( R 2 = 0.34). These empirical relationships can guide budget decisions. They support the conclusion that effective university R&D is fostered by a holistic framework espousing scholarship through research, teaching, and public service benefiting state-scale populations, and are currently at risk.

title: Scientific mobility, prestige and topic alignment in research institutions
authors: Márcia R. Ferreira; Rodrigo Costas; Vito D. P. Servedio; Stefan Thurner
abstract: Abstract Research institutions are crucial in driving intellectual, social, and technological progress. Their ability to innovate depends mainly on their ability to attract, retain, and nurture scientific talent, ultimately making it available to other organizations, industries, or the economy. As researchers change institutions during their careers, their research topics also shift. The extent and mechanisms by which research institutions manage their internal portfolio of scientific topics through the attraction and deployment of researchers are far from well understood. We examine 25 million publication histories of 9.2 million scientists extracted from a large-scale bibliographic database covering thousands of research institutions worldwide to understand how the topics of mobile scientists align with those present in-house. We find a correlation between top-ranked institutions and greater topic alignment, i.e., the degree to which topics of incoming academics match those of their colleagues at the institution. We uncover a similarly high level of alignment among scientists leaving top-ranked institutions. The alignment of research topics in research institutions is more pronounced in engineering, life, health, earth, and physical sciences than in mathematics, computer science, social sciences, and the humanities. We show that institutions have generally become more closely aligned in their overall topic profile over the past two decades. We interpret these results in terms of the levels of proactive management of the composition of the scientific workforce and internal collaboration strategies at the institutional level.

title: The impact of changing metrics in Shanghai Ranking’s Global Ranking of Academic Subjects on medical sciences subjects
authors: Zsolt Kohus; Gergely Ferenc Lendvai
abstract: Abstract This article examines the longitudinal stability, internal consistency, and stratifying effects of Shanghai Ranking’s Global Ranking of Academic Subjects (Shanghai GRAS) in six subjects of Medical Sciences (2017–2025). While Shanghai GRAS has gained prominence as a global higher education benchmark, little is known about the empirical consequences of its methodological changes. Using a quantitative approach combining descriptive statistics, indicator score and overall score change analysis, and K-means clustering, we evaluated the effects of indicator revisions, weight adjustments, and new data sources on institutional trajectories. Our findings show that global methodological alterations influencing all subjects generate substantial volatility, especially for institutions outside the top clusters. The 2019 Category Normalized Citation Impact revision corresponded with overall score increases, while the 2024 methodology restructuring led to significant score declines in general, but the rankings of leading institutions either improved or were not affected. Our findings challenge assumptions about the comparability of rankings and reveal their performative role in reinforcing institutional hierarchies, while also calling for more transparent, context-sensitive evaluation frameworks that reflect the epistemic diversity of global academia.

title: Pink queue and double standard: new evidence on gender gaps from the Italian academia
authors: Marianna Brunetti; Annalisa Fabretti
abstract: Abstract Gender disparities in academic careers remain pronounced, particularly in access to the highest ranks. This paper provides new evidence on these inequalities by modeling academic career progression as a dynamic process. Using a Markov multi-state model, we analyze transitions across academic ranks for the entire population of professors employed in Italian universities between 2016 and 2021. This approach allows us to estimate not only promotion probabilities, but also the expected time required to reach Full professorship. We find that women reach promotion with lower probability and in more years than men, even after accounting for their scientific research output, seniority, and willingness to compete. Although gender gaps narrow when considering an entire career horizon, they never disappear. Importantly, we document that women with a given level of research performance display promotion probabilities systematically similar to those of men with lower research performance, suggesting unequal returns to merit, mirroring other double standards observed in other sectors of the labor market. Our analysis also shows that for women it takes systematically more time to get promotion, a result labeled as pink queue. This study contributes both substantively, by providing a comprehensive assessment of gender disparities in academia, and methodologically, by demonstrating the value of dynamic multi-state models to enrich the study of career progression in structured labor markets.

title: The field-weighted citation impact metric does not adequately account for publication age
authors: Brett P. Dyer
abstract: Abstract To investigate the association between publication month and field-weighted citation impact (FWCI), a cross-sectional study was conducted using 2.1 million medical publications from SciVal, from the 10 countries with the most publications, during 2019–2023. Publications from January and December were excluded due to inaccurate recording of publication dates in SciVal. Quantile regression was used to estimate the association between publication month and FWCI quantiles (50th, 75th, 95th, and 99th percentiles) for 2019–2023 and each separate year. Median FWCI decreased, on average, by 0.030 per month (95% CI: 0.029, 0.031). The equivalent FWCI decreases for the 75th, 95th, and 99th percentiles were 0.067 (95% CI: 0.066, 0.068), 0.232 (95% CI: 0.227, 0.237), and 0.580 (95% CI: 0.553, 0.607), respectively. The median FWCI in November (0.46) was 39% less than the median FWCI in February (0.75). The strength of association between publication month and FWCI percentile was stronger for more recent publication years. When using data for 2023, the median FWCI decreased, on average, by 0.065 per month (95% CI: 0.064, 0.066), compared to 0.017 per month (95% CI: 0.016, 0.018) when using data from 2019. The median FWCI in November 2023 was 64% less than the median FWCI in February 2023, compared to 28% for the equivalent difference in 2019. These findings demonstrate a strong association between FWCI and the month of publication. FWCI is a biased indicator of research impact and needs to account for publication-age dependence by comparing articles from the same month, not only the same year.
